verses.text: Once the call was made to sail for Italy, they put Paul and some other prisoners in the hands of Julius, a centurion from the Imperial Regiment.
We boarded an Adramyttium ship headed for ports along Asia’s coast. Aristarchus, a Macedonian from Thessalonica, came along too.
Next day we docked at Sidon. Julius treated Paul well and let him go see his friends, so they could look after him.
We pushed off again and sailed in Cyprus’s shelter, because the winds were coming straight at us.
After crossing the sea off Cilicia and Pamphylia, we reached Myra in Lycia.
There the centurion found an Alexandrian ship sailing for Italy and moved us aboard.
We crawled along for many days, barely making it across from Cnidus. The wind blocked our way, so we hugged Crete’s shelter, past Salmone.
We struggled along the coast until we reached Fair Havens, near Lasea.
A lot of time had passed, and sailing was getting risky—the Fast was already over. Paul gave them a heads-up:
“Men, I can see this trip is headed for damage and serious loss—not just the cargo and ship, but our lives too.”
But the centurion listened to the captain and shipowner instead of taking Paul’s warning seriously.

The harbor wasn’t good for wintering, so most people said, “Let’s sail on and see if we can reach Phoenix.” It was a Cretan port that faced southwest and northwest, and they wanted to spend winter there.
A gentle south wind came up. Thinking they had the break they needed, they pulled anchor and sailed close along Crete.
But it didn’t take long for a violent wind called Euroclydon to slam down from the island.
The ship got caught and couldn’t face into the wind, so we gave in and let it drive us.
We sailed under the shelter of a little island called Clauda and, with a struggle, managed to secure the lifeboat.
After hauling it aboard, they wrapped cables around the ship to hold it together. Afraid we’d hit the Syrtis sandbars, they lowered the sea anchor and let the storm push us along.
The storm kept hammering us, so the next day they started tossing cargo overboard.
On day three, they threw the ship’s gear into the sea with their own hands.
For days we saw no sun or stars. The storm would not let up, and at last all hope of making it out alive was gone.
After going a long time without food, Paul stood up among them: “Men, you should’ve listened and stayed away from Crete. We wouldn’t be dealing with this damage and loss now.
“But don’t give up! Not one of you will lose your life. Only the ship will be lost.
“Last night an angel from the God I belong to and serve stood right beside me
“and said, ‘Don’t be afraid, Paul. You have to stand before Caesar. God has spared everyone sailing with you.’
“So take heart, everyone! I trust God; it’ll happen exactly as he told me.
“But we’re going to run aground on an island.”
On the fourteenth night, as the storm tossed us around in the Adriatic Sea, the sailors sensed around midnight that land was near.
They took soundings: twenty fathoms. A little later they checked again: fifteen.
Afraid we’d crash into rocks, they dropped four anchors from the stern and waited hard for daylight.
The sailors tried to slip away. They lowered the lifeboat into the sea, pretending they were putting anchors out from the bow.
Paul told the centurion and soldiers, “If these men don’t stay on the ship, none of you can make it.”
So the soldiers cut the lifeboat ropes and let it drift off.
Just before dawn, Paul urged everybody to eat: “You’ve been waiting and fasting for fourteen days now. You haven’t eaten a thing.
“Please eat something. You need it to survive. Not one hair on your head will be lost.”
After saying that, he took bread, thanked God in front of everybody, broke it, and started eating.
That gave them all a lift, and they ate too.
There were 276 people on board altogether.
When they’d eaten enough, they lightened the ship by dumping the wheat into the sea.
When daylight came, they didn’t recognize the coastline, but spotted a bay with a beach and decided to try steering the ship ashore.
They cut loose the anchors and left them at sea, untied the rudder ropes, hoisted the foresail into the wind, and made for the beach.
But they hit a sandbar where two currents met and got the ship stuck. The bow jammed fast; the stern started getting smashed apart by the waves.
The soldiers planned to kill the prisoners so none could swim off and escape.
But the centurion wanted Paul safe, so he stopped them. He ordered the swimmers to jump overboard first and make for shore,
and everybody else to follow on planks or pieces of the wreck. That’s how every person made it safely to land. 🙌
